steps.body: To go the other way, count every piece. Take 2 3/5 — that's **2 whole pizzas plus 3 more fifths.** Each whole pizza is 5 fifths, so 2 wholes = 2×5=10 fifths. Add the extra 3 fifths: 10+3=13 fifths. So 2 3/5 = **13/5.**

widget.prompt: Match each mixed number to its improper fraction.

pairErrors.feedback: 14/3 belongs to 4 2/3. For 1 5/6: 1 whole is 6 sixths, plus 5 more is 11 sixths: 11/6.

widget.missFeedback: Multiply the whole number by the denominator (counting the whole pieces), then add the extra numerator.
widget.successFeedback: 3×4+1=13, 1×6+5=11, 4×3+2=14 — every whole gets counted in pieces, then the extra joins in.

predict.prompt: In 2¾, how many FOURTHS are hiding inside just the 2 wholes?
predict.reveal: Every whole shatters into four fourths — two wholes carry eight of them before the ¾ even joins. That unpacking is the mixed-to-improper move.

explanationVariants: 2 wholes of eighths is 2×8=16 eighths; plus the extra 7 gives 16+7=23 eighths.

widget.prompt: Convert 2 7/8 to an improper fraction. Break every whole into eighths.

commonResults.feedback: Nothing has been broken yet — this is still 2 wholes and 7 eighths. Each whole trades for 8 eighths, so both wholes must come apart.
One whole is still whole. 15/8 counts the eighths from only ONE trade — break the second whole too, and 8 more eighths join: 23/8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the whole number (2) by the denominator (8), then add the extra numerator (7).
widget.successFeedback: 2 7/8 = 23/8 — each whole traded for 8 eighths, so 8 + 8 + 7 = 23 eighths in all.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents mixed to improper.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for mixed to improper must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines mixed to improper.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: That's the rule, named: **whole × denominator + numerator**, all over the same denominator. It isn't a trick to memorize — it's just counting every piece: the whole pizzas' worth, plus the leftover slice.

explanationVariants: 5 wholes of halves is 5×2=10 halves; plus the extra 1 gives 11 halves.

widget.prompt: Convert 5 1/2 to an improper fraction. What is the new numerator (over 2)?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 is only the whole pieces (5×2) — the extra 1 still needs adding: 10+1=11.
6 adds 5+1 instead of multiplying first. It's 5×2=10, then 10+1=11.

widget.prompt: Build the expression that converts 4 2/3 to an improper fraction: whole × denominator + numerator.

commonBuilds.feedback: The multiplication should be whole × denominator (4×3), and the addition should bring in the numerator (2) — not swap their places.

widget.missFeedback: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator.
widget.successFeedback: 4×3+2=14 — every whole counted in thirds, plus the extra two thirds.

explanationVariants: 3 wholes of fourths is 3×4=12 fourths; plus the extra 1 gives 13 fourths.

widget.prompt: A student writes (3 × 4) + 1 for 3 1/4. What improper-fraction numerator does this make?

commonErrors.feedback: 12 is only the whole pieces (3×4) — the extra 1 still needs adding: 12+1=13.
7 adds 3+4 instead of multiplying the whole by the denominator. It's 3×4=12, then 12+1=13.

hints: Multiply the whole number (3) by the denominator (5).
explanationVariants: 3 wholes of fifths is 3×5=15 fifths; plus the extra 2 gives 17 fifths.

widget.prompt: A board is 3 2/5 meters long. As an improper fraction (over 5), what is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 15 is only the whole pieces (3×5) — the extra 2 still needs adding: 15+2=17.
8 adds 3+5 instead of multiplying first. It's 3×5=15, then 15+2=17.

takeaways: Multiply the whole number by the denominator to count the whole pieces.
Add the numerator for the extra pieces.
Keep the same denominator throughout — it's the only piece size in play.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator.** For 2 1/3: 2×3=6 (the whole pieces), plus 1 more gives 7. So 2 1/3 = 7/3.

explanationVariants: 2 wholes of thirds is 6 thirds, plus 1 more is 7 thirds.

options.feedback: 6 is only the whole pieces (2×3) — the extra 1 still needs adding: 7/3.
That drops the whole number entirely. 2×3=6, plus 1 more is 7: 7/3.
